consensus_summary: Across all three blind responses, 'works' are a person's deeds or conduct functioning as the outward expression and evidence of the inner spiritual state: good works are the fruit of faith/grace (often described as acts of obedience, love, and mercy), evil works the fruit of unbelief or the flesh, and works are the basis of divine assessment at judgment. The main disputes are soteriological (evidential vs. cooperative role in justification) and lexical for Paul ('works of the law' as Torah boundary markers vs. moral effort generally).
book_summary: The book identifies works simply as deeds, but insists that 'works' is not a synonym for obedience: a work only becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command, and becomes disobedience when it conflicts with God's command. It further holds that even complete obedience earns no wage (the unprofitable-servant principle of Luke 17), reading Romans 4 as wage/debt vocabulary and James 2 as Abraham's work making faith visible. It rejects the common teaching that Paul's 'works' broadly bundles human obedience and effort as a category set against faith.
consensus_core_identification: Works = human deeds/actions that manifest and evidence the inner spiritual condition, with good works commonly equated with obedience and the fruit of faith, and evil works with sin and unbelief.
book_core_identification: Works = deeds simpliciter, categorically distinct from obedience; a deed acquires the status of obedience or disobedience only relative to a legitimate command, and even perfect obedience earns no wage or merit.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus (especially Response B) folds obedience into good works ('acts of obedience, love, justice, and mercy') and, per the book's own common-view note, reads Paul's 'works' as broadly covering human obedience and effort opposed to faith. The book severs this equation: works and obedience are distinct categories, with obedience being a relational status a work acquires only under a legitimate command. It thereby reclassifies cases the consensus treats as interchangeable — deeds commonly labeled 'obedience' remain works unless command-executing, and Paul's works/wages vocabulary (Rom 4) is narrowed to a labor-for-wages frame rather than a blanket category of human effort. It also excludes any merit-earning reading of even complete obedience (Luke 17:7-10), tightening a boundary the Catholic/Orthodox alternative in the consensus leaves open.
material_contradiction: None at the core. Both sides identify works as human deeds. The book does not replace the referent; it disputes the boundary between works and obedience and the wage/merit implications, which contradicts one listed alternative (cooperative-meritorious works) and the common Pauline framing, but not the consensus's central identification of works as deeds.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus's central referent — works are deeds — so DIVERGENT is inappropriate. But the disagreement is more than wording: it materially changes the conceptual structure by denying the works-obedience synonymy that runs through the consensus responses and the common-view note, by making obedience a conditional status of a work relative to a command, and by asserting that even complete obedience earns nothing (undercutting both the merit alternative and the loose 'obedience and effort vs. faith' framing of Paul). This is real boundary and classification disagreement within the same category, which fits REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the deed-referent and the faith-made-visible reading of James 2 are squarely within consensus territory.
strongest_objection: One could argue this is merely a MATCH with terminological precision: all consensus responses already define works as deeds, none formally asserts that works and obedience are strictly synonymous, and the Luke 17 no-wage point is compatible with the mainstream Protestant evidential view; on this reading the book adds a scholastic distinction without materially altering extension. Against this, the book explicitly frames its distinction against what is 'commonly taught' about Paul's works vocabulary, indicating an intended substantive boundary correction rather than mere restatement.
